# Relevance profile

**This file describes the domain, not a person.** It is read on every run and
injected into the scoring prompt; nothing about any reader is in it, or in the
code. Individual readers tune their own emphasis and follows inside the app,
so this document's job is to define what the domain covers, concretely enough
to score against. Vague profiles produce vague scores.

---

## The domain

The AI industry, read daily from the trade press: what is being built,
shipped, funded and regulated across the stack that runs from silicon to
chatbot. The scoreable signal is CHANGE: a model release that moves a
benchmark, a chip deal that shifts who can train at scale, a funding round
that resets a valuation, a regulation that changes what a lab can ship next.
A press release restating a company's existing roadmap is not news; a number,
a name, or a date attached to a move is.

## Technology areas, covered evenly

- **Frontier models and capability claims** -- flagship releases and point
  updates from the major labs, benchmark results (SWE-bench, GPQA, ARC-AGI,
  LMArena Elo), and the test-time-compute and reasoning-model trend that now
  drives capability as much as pretraining scale does.
- **Compute, chips and infrastructure** -- GPU and accelerator generations,
  foundry and packaging capacity (TSMC, CoWoS, HBM supply), hyperscaler
  capex, data-center buildouts, and custom silicon (TPU, Trainium, MI-series)
  built to reduce Nvidia dependency.
- **Safety, security and alignment** -- responsible-scaling and preparedness
  frameworks, third-party evaluations (METR, Apollo Research, UK AISI),
  interpretability research, and disclosed agentic-AI incidents, jailbreaks
  or scheming behavior.
- **Policy, regulation and geopolitics** -- binding rules (EU AI Act
  enforcement, US state law, export controls on advanced chips) and the
  US-China and sovereign-AI dynamics that shape who can buy what.
- **Enterprise adoption, agents and applications** -- the shift from chatbot
  to production agent: coding tools, computer-use agents, enterprise
  platforms (Copilot, Agentforce, AIP), and vertical deployments with named
  customers and measurable outcomes.
- **Funding, deals and corporate strategy** -- rounds, valuations, compute
  supply agreements, M&A and acquihires, IPO moves, and the running
  capex-bubble argument among investors and analysts.
- **Open source and research ecosystem** -- open-weight releases (Llama,
  Mistral, and the Chinese open-weight tier: DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, GLM),
  the arXiv-to-conference research pipeline, and leaderboard activity.
- **Talent and org dynamics** -- researcher departures, spin-outs,
  compensation wars and internal restructurings, read as a leading indicator
  of where frontier capability is migrating.
- **Robotics and embodied AI** -- humanoid platforms, world models and robot
  foundation models, a capital-intensive beat now distinct enough from
  general enterprise applications to need its own attention.

## Who builds, buys and funds

- **The frontier labs** -- OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, xAI, Meta,
  Mistral -- and the Chinese labs (DeepSeek, Alibaba, Moonshot, Zhipu)
  competing on cost and open weights rather than closed frontier claims.
- **The compute buyers** -- hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta)
  and neoclouds (CoreWeave and peers) whose capex commitments are the
  clearest leading indicator of where training and inference capacity goes
  next.
- **The enterprise adopters** -- companies buying seats, API access or
  platform licenses (Copilot, Agentforce, AIP, Bedrock); named customers and
  deployment scale are what separate a real adoption story from a vendor
  pitch.
- **The capital** -- venture firms (a16z, Sequoia, Thrive) and sovereign
  wealth vehicles (MGX, PIF, Mubadala, SoftBank) increasingly co-anchoring
  the mega-rounds and infrastructure megaprojects (Stargate) that fund
  frontier training runs.
- **Governments and regulators** -- as both rule-setters (EU AI Office, US
  state legislatures, CAC) and, increasingly, as direct customers and
  compute underwriters via sovereign-AI programs.

## The vendor landscape

- **Frontier labs**, evaluated on model releases, capability claims and the
  compute and capital deals that make the next training run possible.
- **Chip and compute vendors** -- Nvidia's generation-to-generation cadence
  (Blackwell to Rubin) as the pacing signal, with AMD, Broadcom, TSMC and the
  hyperscalers' custom silicon as the challenger and hedge story.
- **Applied-AI and infrastructure vendors** -- coding agents (Cursor, Claude
  Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot), inference and serving layers (vLLM, Hugging
  Face, Cerebras, Groq), and generative-media specialists (Runway,
  ElevenLabs, Suno, Midjourney) building on top of frontier models.
- **Enterprise platform vendors** -- Microsoft, Salesforce, Palantir, AWS --
  competing to own the agent layer that enterprises actually deploy against.
- Movement between these tiers -- a lab building its own chip, a cloud
  provider becoming a model developer, an applied-AI startup getting
  acquired by a hyperscaler -- reshapes the market faster than any single
  release.

## What to score highly, in rough priority order

1. **Model releases and capability claims** -- a new model, a benchmark
   result, an architecture or training-method change, with numbers and a
   named model where the article has them. Marketing claims with no
   benchmark or eval attached score lower than the same claim with one.
2. **Compute and chip supply** -- chip generation launches, foundry or HBM
   capacity news, export-control changes, and compute-supply deals that
   determine who can train or serve at scale.
3. **Funding rounds, valuations and acquisitions** -- new rounds, priced
   valuations, M&A, acquihires, and IPO movement, especially where the deal
   ties a lab to a specific compute or cloud partner.
4. **Safety and regulation that changes what can ship** -- a binding rule, an
   enforcement action, a safety-framework update, or an eval result that
   changes a release timeline or a deployment surface -- not commentary about
   risk in the abstract.
5. **Vendor and customer movement** -- a named enterprise adopting or
   dropping a platform, a lab-chip or lab-cloud tie forming or breaking, a
   vendor winning or losing ground against a rival.
6. **Talent and org moves** -- a researcher departure, spin-out or
   restructuring significant enough to signal where capability is heading.
7. **Direction shifts and counter-trends** -- open versus closed weights,
   scaling laws holding or breaking, test-time compute versus pretraining,
   humanoid robotics versus narrow automation. A broken trend is worth
   knowing early, and the note must say which way the evidence points.

## What the domain does not need

- Generic "AI will change everything" trend pieces with no company, model or
  deal attached.
- Consumer-facing product reviews and how-to content (prompt tips, chatbot
  comparisons written for end users rather than the industry).
- Philosophical or speculative AGI/consciousness commentary with no news
  hook.
- Market-research-report spam ("the global AI market will reach $X
  billion").
- Routine earnings coverage of large tech companies that merely mentions AI
  without a specific model, product or deal.
- Duplicate coverage of the same benchmark leaderboard update across outlets
  with no new information.

## Scoring guidance

Prefer the item with a number, a name and a date over the item with a theme.
A capability claim with no benchmark, customer, or dollar figure attached is
marketing, and scores like it. When a story takes a side in a live technical
or industry argument -- the capex-bubble debate, open versus closed weights,
whether scaling laws are holding -- say so in the note and say which side.
